summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base for managing the Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) protocol for IPv4. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2934 gives network managers a standard set of values to read from a router that runs Protocol Independent Multicast for IPv4. The values cover the router's PIM interfaces, its PIM neighbours, its multicast routes and the rendezvous points it knows about, and some of them can be changed to configure PIM.

questions: how to monitor pim with snmp
is the pim mib for ipv6
subtitle: The SNMP objects a router exposes so an operator can see and configure IPv4 Protocol Independent Multicast.

tldr.problem: Operators of IPv4 multicast routers had no standard set of values they could read over SNMP to see how Protocol Independent Multicast was running on a router.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a MIB module written in SMIv2, holding one scalar and eight tables: interfaces, neighbors, multicast routes, next hops, rendezvous points, candidate rendezvous points and PIM components.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document. It covers IPv4 only, and some of its objects are marked deprecated because they exist to manage PIM version 1 routers, although PIM version 1 was itself obsoleted by PIM version 2.

today: RFC 2934 is an Experimental document from October 2000, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the values a router may expose for managing PIM for IPv4, and the module keeps a set of deprecated objects so that PIM version 1 routers can still be managed even though PIM version 1 itself was obsoleted by PIM version 2.

sections.title: What This MIB Manages
sections.content:
RFC 2934 defines a portion of the Management Information Base, the store of named values that network management protocols read and write. It describes managed objects used for managing the Protocol Independent Multicast protocol for IPv4, and it applies to IPv4 multicast routers that implement PIM.

The memo states a limit on its scope: this MIB does not support management of PIM for other address families, including IPv6. Such management may be supported by other MIBs.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds standard values to the set a manager can read from a router. It covers routers that run PIM for IPv4 only, and says nothing about managing PIM for IPv6.

sections.title: The SNMP Network Management Framework
sections.content:
The memo sets out the framework the new objects sit in, which has five parts: an overall architecture, described in RFC 2271; mechanisms for describing and naming objects and events for the purpose of management, called the Structure of Management Information, in its first version SMIv1 and its second version SMIv2; message protocols for transferring management information, namely SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3; protocol operations for accessing management information; and a set of fundamental applications together with the view-based access control mechanism.

Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base, and objects in it are defined using the mechanisms of the SMI. The memo specifies a module that complies with SMIv2. A module conforming to SMIv1 can be produced through the appropriate translations, and the translated MIB must be semantically equivalent, except where objects or events are omitted because no translation is possible, which the memo names as the use of Counter64. Some machine readable information in SMIv2 becomes textual description in SMIv1 during translation, and the memo says this loss of machine readable information is not considered to change the semantics of the MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP already has a standard way of naming and describing the values a device exposes. This memo writes the new values in that same language, and says how to convert them for older versions of the language.

sections.title: One Scalar and Eight Tables
sections.content:
The module contains one scalar, pimJoinPruneInterval, which is the default interval at which periodic PIM Sparse Mode Join/Prune messages are sent, and eight tables. Some of the objects in these tables are deprecated. The memo keeps them because they are necessary for managing PIM version 1 routers, and it notes that PIM version 1 is itself obsoleted by PIM version 2.

The tables cover the router's PIM interfaces, its PIM neighbors, its multicast routing entries, the next hops in those entries, rendezvous points in both the deprecated version 1 form and the version 2 RP-Set form, the groups for which the local router advertises itself as a candidate rendezvous point, and the PIM domains the router is connected to. The module sits at experimental 61 in the object identifier tree, with the objects under pimMIBObjects 1 and the notification under pimMIBObjects 0.
sections.plainLanguage: The module holds one setting and eight lists. Each list is a table of related values the router keeps, such as its PIM interfaces or its PIM neighbours. The tables are numbered from 2 to 12 in the object identifier tree.

sections.title: Interfaces, Neighbors and Routes
sections.content:
The Interface table has one row per PIM interface, indexed by pimInterfaceIfIndex. It records the interface's IP address and network mask, the Designated Router on that interface, which is 0.0.0.0 on point-to-point interfaces, and the interval at which PIM Hello messages are transmitted, which defaults to 30 seconds. The mode of an interface is one of three values, and a value of sparseDense is only valid for PIM version 1. Creating a row enables PIM on the interface and destroying the row disables PIM there.

The Neighbor table has one row per PIM neighbor, indexed by the neighbor's address, with the interface used to reach it, how long it has been a neighbor, and the minimum time remaining before it is aged out. The IP Multicast Route table has one row per multicast routing entry whose incoming interface is running PIM, and it exposes the PIM-specific flags for the entry, the RPT and SPT bits. The Next Hop table covers the outgoing interface list entries whose interface runs PIM and whose state is pruned, and records why each was pruned: other, prune in response to a PIM prune message, or assert from PIM Assert processing. The RP-Set table holds version 2 information about sets of candidate rendezvous points for group address prefixes. The Candidate-RP table lists the groups for which the local router advertises itself as a candidate rendezvous point, and if that table is empty the router advertises itself for all groups. The Component table has one row for each PIM domain the router is connected to, and a PIM-SM domain is defined as an area of the network over which Bootstrap messages are forwarded.

The module also defines one notification, pimNeighborLoss, which signals the loss of an adjacency with a neighbor. It should be generated when the neighbor timer expires and the router has no other neighbors on the same interface with a lower IP address than itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Each table answers a question an operator asks: which interfaces run PIM, which routers are PIM neighbours, which streams pass through here, and which routers act as meeting points for a group. The router also sends an alert when it loses a PIM neighbour.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo notes that many of the objects in the module can be read, some can be written, and the ones with read-write or read-create access let an administrator configure PIM in the router. Unauthorized access to the readable objects is relatively innocuous, but unauthorized access to the writable objects could cause a denial of service, so support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

The memo says SNMPv1 by itself is such an insecure environment. Even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPSEC, there is then no control over who on the secure network is allowed to access and change the objects in this MIB. It recommends that implementers consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, specifically the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model. It then places the remaining duty on the customer or user: to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to this MIB is properly configured to give access to those objects only to those principals that have legitimate rights to access them.
sections.plainLanguage: Reading these values is mostly harmless, but letting an unauthorized manager change them could break the router's multicast forwarding. The memo recommends the security features of SNMP version 3 and leaves the task of restricting access to the operator.

viz.caption: THE EIGHT TABLES IN THE PIM MIB

cells: each PIM interface of the router
each PIM neighbor of the router
each multicast routing entry whose incoming interface runs PIM
each outgoing interface list entry whose interface runs PIM and whose state is pruned
the PIM version 1 information common to all RPs of a group
the PIM version 2 candidate RP sets for group address prefixes
the groups for which the router advertises itself as a Candidate-RP
each PIM domain the router is connected to
